City officials and the site planner agreed that storm drainage from the site should be run to the lake, but the planner was concerned that hydrocarbons, salt and other pollutants from the roads and parking lots on the site could contaminate the lake and water supply. The soil is very permeable under the site area, and provides filtration of water percolating through it.
The planner therefore designed the storm system using leaching catch basins which have open bottoms, with discharge outlets some distance above the bottom of the inlets so that the first surge of storm water runoff would not pass through the system to the lake, but go directly into the soil, utilizing the filtration power of the granular soil to remove as much as possible of the pollutants picked up from the paved surfaces. Also, open spaces were graded in a manner similar to that used at Indianapolis to serve as holding basins to minimize early runoff and any erosion of the hillside slope.
Consideration was also given to the potential siltation of the lake from storm runoff and erosion during construction. As noted earlier, housing construction was held back from the ridge line in order to minimize this problem, and straw bales were used with controlled fill as necessary to block erosion of the hillside.
King County: The King County site experiences the typical rainy season of the Seattle area. The primary surface drainage path runs through the site, which has served as a natural holding basin for this flow. The site planner has worked with the appropriate County officials to develop alternate drainage methods and to provide additional drainage structures in order to minimize the impact of this site construction on the overall drainage problem.
Macon: The Macon site includes and surrounds a small lake, which is spring-fed from the site area. It was noted earlier that the alluvial area and spring locations have been retained as open space in the site plan. Drainage considerations similar to those at Kalamazoo guided the design of the Macon site drainage system, with first runoff being directed away from the lake. Also at Macon, a siphon system has been constructed to provide a "turnover" in the lake water in order to prevent eutrophication. In order to measure the effectiveness of this effort, the Bibb County Planning Commission is undertaking for HUD two studies at the site: (1) An ecological study to determine if a small, wild area (natural habitat) can be maintained within an urban center if an urban population can be educated to take an interest in such an area and help preserve it and (2) an assessment of the effects of planned urban development on the quality of existing surface water on the site before, during, and after construction and occupation of housing units.
